Such a curve supplies phase points; if a configuration domain admits no points there is no such curve and these conditional claims are vacuous. Step 2.2 uses the full momentum fibre over each actual x, which contains the explicitly specified zero momentum p=0, to define g(t,x)=f(t,x,0). It selects no element from an empty fibre.

The Statement for the forced Hamiltonian field imposes no nonzero phase-value condition: zero momentum and zero tangent values are allowed at admissible base points, and its algebraic formulas apply there. A zero configuration is included only when it lies in the declared chart, so no origin outside the domain is claimed.
Statement allows N=1 and steps 1.1–1.4 use the same three-component Cartesian field and forced momentum equations; a one-coordinate immersion separately yields the scalar chart equation of step 1.3.

Statement clause 4 requires an exact velocity-independent residual potential on Q, not mere independence of velocity. Step 2.2 proves necessity with V=g-U and identifies the componentwise additive time freedom; step 1.5 proves sufficiency. Nonexact closed residual forces therefore remain excluded.

boundaries.reason: The Statement for the forced Hamiltonian field is local on its declared chart and time domain; it makes no terminal boundary-value prescription or extension outside that domain.
Step 2.2 constructs the residual potential as g-U with g(t,x)=f(t,x,0); no primitives are chosen on unrelated domains. Component-dependent time additions are precisely the declared gauge freedom.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–1.4 and 2.1 identify the motion, momentum and integral-curve formulations. In clause 4, step 2.2 takes a Hamiltonian forced field to the exact residual potential V=g-U, with componentwise time gauge freedom.

Steps 1.1–1.4 express the Hamilton systems back as the model and Lagrange equations. For clause 4, step 1.5 starts with the exact residual potential and constructs f=H+V, whose field is exactly the forced field.

risk_review.notes: Read all eight steps and exact CM12 hyperregularity/equivalence, motions, potential-normalization, field and zero-derivative supplier statements. Clauses 1-3 retain their independent hypotheses: d=0 for unforced motions, declared Lagrange equations for any immersion rather than unconstrained ambient equations. Necessity in clause 4 integrates the p-gradient on the entire convex momentum fiber and sets g(t,x)=f(t,x,0), preserving joint C2 regularity; V=g-U is global and velocity independent. Sufficiency uses H+V. Gauge functions are independent on open connected components; no closed-to-exact assertion or existence/completeness claim. Reader joint-C2 convention makes the quantified phase function explicit without changing autonomous consumer uses.

citations.quote:
Adopt one force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ particle labels
with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ (clause (i)), an open nondegenerate time
window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
and a force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ and identify position tuples with points of
$\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]); dimensions are
read by [[def-cm01-units]], inner products and norms are Euclidean
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\mathsf M$ be the mass
operator of clause (d) of [[def-cm01-configuration]],
$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N})$, a symmetric
positive definite linear map of $\mathbb R^{3N}$.

**(a) Kinetic energy.** The **kinetic energy** of the labels at coordinate
velocity $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}=\mathbb R^{3N}$ is

$$K(v):=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_{i}\,\lvert v_{i}\rvert_{2}^{2}=\frac12\,v\cdot\mathsf M v .$$

$K$ is the restriction of a $C^{\infty}$ function of $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy). Its Euclidean gradient is
$K'(v)=\mathsf M v$, because $\partial K/\partial v_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

**(b) Mechanical Lagrangian of a potential presentation.** Let $(U,d)$ be a
potential presentation of the model's force map in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]: a function
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ with dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d=(d_{1},\dots,d_{N})$ such that
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)$$
on the state domain. The **mechanical Lagrangian of the presentation** is

$$L:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad L(t,x,v):=K(v)-U(t,x).$$

$L$ is of class $C^{2}$ on its open domain and has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
When $d\equiv0$ the presentation is a global potential model and $L$ is a
Lagrangian of the model itself; when $d\not\equiv0$, $L$ carries the potential
part only, and the residual force contribution $d$ is not included in $L$.
The
potential representative is part of the declared data: replacing $U$ by
$U+c(t)$ for differentiable $c:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c)).

**(c) Action, variations, stationarity.** Let $a<b$ be reals with
$[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$. If $Q=\varnothing$, there is no map
$x:[a,b]\to Q$, so this clause has no action, variation or stationarity
instance. Assume $Q\ne\varnothing$ for the chart construction below, and put
$O:=I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. The set $O$ is open and contains
$[a,b]\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, so with $n:=3N$ the pair $(O,L)$ is a
time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times Q$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]. **Admissible
curves** (the $C^{2}$ curves $x:[a,b]\to Q$ with the extension convention of
that definition), **variations** $\eta$ with $\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0$, the
**action**

$$S(x):=\int_{a}^{b}L\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\,dt,$$

the **first variation** $\delta S(x)[\eta]$ and **stationarity** of $x$ are the
notions of [[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] instantiated at this
chart; the derivative $x'$ is the coordinate velocity ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).
The action has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (energy multiplied by time).
Write $E_{L}(x):[a,b]\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ for the Euler-Lagrange expression of
the instantiated chart.

**(d) Status.** This item defines the action functional and the Lagrangian of a
presentation from data already adopted in the model: no new force law, no
equation of motion and no measured value are introduced. The first variation
of $S$ exists for every admissible curve and variation and its formula, the
equivalence of stationarity with the vanishing of $E_{L}(x)$, and the relation
of both to the model's equation of motion are theorems of this page, not part
of the definition.

**Chart data.** Let $n\ge1$, let $a<b$ be reals and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and
nonempty. Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$ be an open set with

$$[a,b]\times U\times\mathbb R^n\subseteq O,$$

and let $\mathcal L:O\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pair $(O,\mathcal L)$ is a **time-dependent
Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$**. The three slots of $\mathcal L$ are written
$(t,q,v)$, so that $t$ is the time, $q$ the configuration and $v$ the velocity; the open set
$O$ has the three coordinate blocks of sizes $1,n,n$.

**Admissible curves and variations.** A map $q:[a,b]\to U$ is **of class $C^2$** when there are
$\varepsilon>0$ and a $C^2$ map $\tilde q:(a-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n$ with
$\tilde q|_{[a,b]}=q$ and $\tilde q(t)\in U$ for every $t\in[a,b]$; the derivative $q'$ and the
second derivative $q''$ below are those of any such extension, and they are independent of the
extension on $[a,b]$. A **variation** of a $C^2$ curve $q$ is a map $\eta:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ of
class $C^2$ in the same sense with

$$\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0 .$$

Thus the admissible curves and variations are the restrictions to $[a,b]$ of $C^2$ maps on a
common open interval, exactly the convention under which $C^2$ data on a closed interval are used
in [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and in the classical treatments cited
below.

**The action.** For a $C^2$ curve $q:[a,b]\to U$ the map $t\mapsto\mathcal L(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is
continuous on $[a,b]$, because $q,q'$ are continuous and $\mathcal L$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); it is therefore Darboux integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). The **action** of $q$ is the real number

$$S(q):=\int_a^b\mathcal L\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\,dt .$$

**First variation.** For a $C^2$ curve $q$ and a variation $\eta$ the curve $q_\varepsilon:=q+\varepsilon\eta$
takes values in $U$ for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$; this is proved in
[[lem-cm-first-variation-formula]] and is *not* part of the present definition. The **first
variation of $S$ at $q$ in the direction $\eta$** is the ordinary two-sided derivative at $\varepsilon=0$
of the function $\varepsilon\mapsto S(q+\varepsilon\eta)$, written

$$\delta S(q)[\eta]:=\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}S(q+\varepsilon\eta),$$

whenever this derivative exists; [[lem-cm-first-variation-formula]] proves that it does exist
under the present hypotheses and computes it, so the notation denotes a single real number for
every pair $(q,\eta)$ arising here.

**Euler–Lagrange expression.** Let $\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\in\mathbb R^n$ and
$\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\in\mathbb R^n$ be the gradients of $\mathcal L$ in the second and third slots
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Since
$\mathcal L$ is $C^2$, the maps $t\mapsto\mathcal L_v(t,q(t),q'(t))$ are $C^1$ and
$t\mapsto\mathcal L_q(t,q(t),q'(t))$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. The **Euler–Lagrange expression of
$\mathcal L$ along $q$** is the continuous map

$$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t):=\mathcal L_q\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)-\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(\mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\Bigr)\in\mathbb R^n.$$

**Stationarity.** A $C^2$ curve $q$ is **stationary for $S$** when

$$\delta S(q)[\eta]=0\qquad\text{for every variation }\eta.$$

**Scope.** The definition introduces only chart data, the action and its first variation. It
asserts nothing about minimising $S$, nothing about the existence of stationary curves and nothing
about any physical interpretation of $\mathcal L$; the equivalence of stationarity with the
vanishing of $E_{\mathcal L}(q)$ is the theorem [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]], and
the distinction between stationary and minimising curves is recorded in
[[rem-cm-scope-of-stationarity]].

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], with configuration domain $Q$, time
window $I_{0}$ and force map $F$. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]
and gradients are Euclidean ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); points of
$Q$ are written $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(a) Potential representation of the force map.** A model **presents its
force map through a potential** when it declares a function
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of class $C^{2}$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules), with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; here $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is the
gradient of $u\mapsto U(t,x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},u,x_{i+1},\dots,x_{N})$ at
$u=x_{i}$. More generally, a model may declare **residual forces**
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the standing
regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and present
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v);$$
the pair $(U,d)$ is then the model's presentation and
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
configuration-space force field** is a $C^{1}$ map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, where
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is the open configuration domain and each
$\varphi_i(x)$ is the force on label $i$ at configuration $x$; its components
have force dimension. It represents a force map of the form
$F_i(t,x,v)=\varphi_i(x)$ on the model's state domain. This configuration-space
field is not in general an external single-label force: to identify its
$i$th component with an external map of [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i),
one must further require that it depend on $x_i$ alone, as in the declared
signature $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_i,v_i)$. Such a field is **closed** when
$\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ for all coordinate indices
$j,k\in\{1,\dots,3N\}$ at every point of $Q$, and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense
of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]]);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

**(f) Equipotential level sets.** Let $U:Q\to\mathbb R$ be $C^{2}$, let
$c\in\mathbb R$ and suppose $U^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$ and $\nabla
U(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in U^{-1}(c)$; equivalently $c$ is a regular value of
$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

**(g) Status.** The potential, its normalization, the residual forces and the
declaration of a potential presentation are model data; the closed/exact
statements of (d)-(f) are cited mathematics about the declared field. This
item asserts no conservation law, no force law of nature and no measured
value.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch the mass metric restricts the
Euclidean inner product to $Q$ as in that item.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** on the open ambient set $O$ is a pair of smooth maps
$$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'\times3N},\qquad b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'},\qquad 1\le k'\le3N,$$
with $A(t,x)$ of constant rank $k'$ everywhere in the declared domain,
imposing $A(t,x(t))\dot x(t)+b(t,x(t))=0$ on a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to O$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval, the parameter $t$ is frame time, and $\dot x(t):=x'(t)$ is the componentwise derivative in the convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Equivalently $A(t,x)$ is a linear map
$\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k'}$. Each row's output unit is declared, and
its corresponding component of $b$ has that same unit. The allowed velocities
at $(t,x)$ form the affine set $\{v:A(t,x)v+b(t,x)=0\}$; its differences form
$\ker A(t,x)$.

The law is **locally holonomic-equivalent at $(t_0,x_0)$** if on some open
neighbourhood $V\subseteq\mathbb R\times O$ of that point there are a $C^2$
map $g:V\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ with $D_xg$ of rank $k'$ and a $C^2$ matrix map
$C:V\to\mathbb R^{k'\times k'}$ with $\det C\ne0$ such that
$$A=C\,D_xg,\qquad b=C\,\partial_tg\qquad\text{on }V.$$
Thus the velocity law is locally the derivative of the regular positional
constraints $g(t,x)=\text{constant}$. It is **locally nonholonomic at the
specified point** when no such neighbourhood and pair $(g,C)$ exists; a
nonholonomic model in this local sense declares a point (or a region of
points) with this failure. For a homogeneous time-independent law this
excludes local position submanifolds whose tangent spaces equal $\ker A$;
for an affine time-dependent law the criterion also includes the drift $b$.
Absence of a single global pair alone does not establish local
nonintegrability. The rank of $A$ counts instantaneous velocity restrictions,
not the dimension of a positional configuration manifold; accessibility
requires its own definition. Rank changes require a separate model.

Adopt one force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ particle
labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ (clause (i)), an open
nondegenerate time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration
domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ and a force map $F$ with the standing
continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause (iii) of that
postulate, and fix one inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]). Adopt in addition a potential presentation
$(U,d)$ of [[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]: a function
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ of dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ with $F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)$,
with residual forces $d=(d_{1},\dots,d_{N})$ of the standing regularity. Let
$L=K-U$, $O:=I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and $\mathsf M$ be the
mechanical Lagrangian, the chart domain and the mass operator of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], so that $L$ is of class $C^{2}$
on the open set $O$; when $Q\ne\varnothing$, $(O,L)$ is a time-dependent
Lagrangian chart over every $[a,b]\times Q$ with $a<b$ and
$[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]], inner products and norms are Euclidean
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For a $C^{1}$ function
$\varphi$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and
$(t,x,v)\in O$ write

$$D_{t}\varphi(t,x,v):=\varphi_{t}(t,x)+\varphi_{x}(t,x)\cdot v,$$

the derivative of $s\mapsto\varphi(s,x+v(s-t))$ at $s=t$; the last two slots
of $L$ are $(x,v)$, and $L_{t}$, $L_{x}$, $L_{v}$ are the gradients of $L$ in
its three slots ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

**(a) Symmetry datum.** A **symmetry datum of the model's mechanical
Lagrangian** is a triple $(\tau,\xi,B)$ of maps

$$\tau:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R,\qquad \xi:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad B:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R,$$

of class $C^{2}$, that satisfies for every $(t,x,v)\in O$ the **Noether
identity of the model**:

$$L_{t}(t,x,v)\,\tau(t,x)+L_{x}(t,x,v)\cdot\xi(t,x)+L_{v}(t,x,v)\cdot\bigl(D_{t}\xi(t,x,v)-v\,D_{t}\tau(t,x,v)\bigr)+L(t,x,v)\,D_{t}\tau(t,x,v)=D_{t}B(t,x,v).$$

Because $K(v)=\tfrac12 v\cdot\mathsf M v$ does not depend on $t$ or $x$ and
$U$ does not depend on $v$, the identity is the following identity among the
model's data:

$$-U_{t}(t,x)\tau(t,x)-\nabla_{x}U(t,x)\cdot\xi(t,x)+\bigl(\mathsf M v\bigr)\cdot\bigl(D_{t}\xi(t,x,v)-v\,D_{t}\tau(t,x,v)\bigr)+\bigl(K(v)-U(t,x)\bigr)D_{t}\tau(t,x,v)=D_{t}B(t,x,v).$$

It involves the declared potential $U$, the masses through $\mathsf M$, and
the boundary function $B$; it is an identity imposed on the model's declared
data on the whole state domain $O$.

**(b) Strict data and point symmetries.** A symmetry datum is **strict**
when $\tau\equiv0$; its identity reads
$L_{x}\cdot\xi+L_{v}\cdot D_{t}\xi=D_{t}B$. The following chart
identification is for $Q\ne\varnothing$. If a strict datum has $\xi$
independent of $t$, then the pair $(\xi,B)$ is an **infinitesimal point
symmetry of the chart $(O,L)$** in the sense of
[[def-cm-infinitesimal-point-symmetry]]: that definition's identity,
instantiated with $n=3N$ in the configuration slot, is verbatim
$L_{x}(t,x,v)\cdot\xi(x)+L_{v}(t,x,v)\cdot D\xi(x)v=B_{t}(t,x)+B_{x}(t,x)\cdot v$.
Conversely every infinitesimal point symmetry of the chart $(O,L)$ whose
generator and boundary function are of class $C^{2}$, with the boundary
function defined on $I_{0}\times Q$, is a strict datum with $\xi$ independent
of $t$. A general datum is a **point symmetry with time
reparametrisation**: the family

$$x_{i}\longmapsto x_{i}+s\,\xi_{i}(t,x),\qquad t\longmapsto t+s\,\tau(t,x)$$

changes the coordinate velocity to first order by $D_{t}\xi-v\,D_{t}\tau$, and
the identity says that the infinitesimal variation of $L$ along the family is
the total time derivative $D_{t}B$ of the chart function $B$.

**(c) Charge.** The **charge of the datum** is the function

$$C:O\to\mathbb R,\qquad C(t,x,v):=L_{v}(t,x,v)\cdot\xi(t,x)-E(t,x,v)\,\tau(t,x)-B(t,x),$$

where

$$E(t,x,v):=L_{v}(t,x,v)\cdot v-L(t,x,v)=K(v)+U(t,x)$$

is the **mechanical energy function of the chart**
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]). Since $L_{v}=\mathsf M v$,

$$C(t,x,v)=\bigl(\mathsf M v\bigr)\cdot\xi(t,x)-\bigl(K(v)+U(t,x)\bigr)\tau(t,x)-B(t,x).$$

**(d) Dimensions and rescaling.** Read the family parameter $s$ as carrying a
declared unit $\sigma$ (for instance radians for a rotation family, seconds
for a time-reparametrisation family, or a dimensionless parameter). Then
$\tau$ has dimension $\tau\sigma^{-1}$, every component
$\xi_{i}$ has dimension $\ell\sigma^{-1}$, $B$ has dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\sigma^{-1}$ (action per parameter unit) and
$C$ has the same dimension as $B$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Replacing $(\tau,\xi,B)$ by $(c\tau,c\xi,cB)$ with
a real constant $c\ne0$ — the same family reparametrised by $s\mapsto cs$ —
rescales $C$ by $c$.

**(e) Status.** This item fixes the model's symmetry vocabulary: which data
satisfy the model's Noether identity, and which function is their charge. It
asserts neither that a given model admits a nonzero symmetry datum, nor that
the charge of a datum is conserved. Conservation is proved under explicit
hypotheses by the theorems of this page, and the hypotheses must be verified
against the declared potential $U$ and the masses: a change of inertial frame,
the affine structure of the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]], or a
relabelling of the particle labels is a kinematic or descriptive operation and
is not by itself a symmetry datum of $L$. Every statement that uses a charge
names the potential representative used
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c)); the effect of
changing the representative is recorded in the general Noether theorem of this
page.

Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $A\subseteq\mathbb R\times V$ be open sets containing respectively the configuration projection of $O$ and its time-configuration projection. Let

$$\xi:V\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad B:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$

be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $D\xi(q)\in M_n(\mathbb R)$
for the Jacobian matrix of $\xi$ at $q$ ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]],
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), and for a $C^1$ function $\varphi(t,q)$ write

$$D_t\varphi(t,q,v):=\varphi_t(t,q)+\varphi_q(t,q)\cdot v .$$

The pair $(\xi,B)$ is an **infinitesimal point symmetry of $\mathcal L$** when the identity

$$\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)+\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot D\xi(q)v =B_t(t,q)+B_q(t,q)\cdot v$$

holds for every $(t,q,v)\in O$. The **charge of the pair** is the function

$$C(t,q,v):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)-B(t,q).$$

**Reading of the identity.** The left-hand side is the derivative of the Lagrangian under the
infinitesimal family of point transformations

$$q\longmapsto q+s\,\xi(q),\qquad t\longmapsto t$$

with the velocity transformed accordingly by $v\mapsto v+s\,D\xi(q)v$, and the right-hand side is
the total derivative $\frac{d}{dt}B(t,q(t))$ along a $C^1$ trajectory with $q'(t)=v$; thus the identity says that the infinitesimal variation of
$\mathcal L$ is a total time derivative of the chart function $B$. In particular:

- Taking $B=0$ reduces the identity to
  $\mathcal L_q(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)+\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot D\xi(q)v=0$, the invariance of
  $\mathcal L$ under the infinitesimal family.
- For a constant field $\xi\equiv a$ one has $D\xi=0$, and the identity reads
  $\mathcal L_q\cdot a=B_t+B_q\cdot v$; when $B$ is independent of $q$ this is the statement that
  $\mathcal L$ is unchanged by the translation $q\mapsto q+sa$ up to a total time derivative.

**Scope.** The definition is an identity imposed on the chart data; it does not assert that a
given Lagrangian possesses any symmetry, nor that a symmetry of the configuration space, a frame
change or any kinematic structure automatically induces one. Whether a symmetry produces a
conserved quantity along the Euler–Lagrange solutions is the theorem
[[thm-cm-point-symmetry-charge-is-conserved]]; the general reparametrisation version is
[[thm-cm-point-noether-identity-with-time-reparametrization]], and the scope of the statement for
physical models is recorded in [[rem-cm-scope-of-point-symmetry]].

Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$, let $(\xi,B)$ be an
infinitesimal point symmetry of $\mathcal L$ with charge $C(t,q,v)=\mathcal L_v(t,q,v)\cdot\xi(q)-B(t,q)$
([[def-cm-infinitesimal-point-symmetry]]), and let $q:I\to U$ be a $C^2$ curve on an open interval
$I\supseteq[a,b]$ with $(t,q(t),q'(t))\in O$ for all $t\in I$ that solves the Euler–Lagrange
equation

$$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$

i.e. $\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal L_v(t,q,q')=\mathcal L_q(t,q,q')$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]], [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]]).
Then the function

$$t\longmapsto C\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)=\mathcal L_v(t,q(t),q'(t))\cdot\xi(q(t))-B(t,q(t))$$

is constant on $I$.

Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] and let $q:[a,b]\to U$ be a $C^2$ admissible curve.
Then $q$ is stationary for the action $S$ if and only if

$$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0\qquad\text{for every }t\in[a,b].$$

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and the mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$ and $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]).
Let $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$, and let $x:[a,b]\to Q$ be a $C^{2}$
admissible curve ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Then the
following three conditions are equivalent:

1. $x$ is stationary for the action $S$ of $L$;
2. $E_{L}(x)(t)=0$ for every $t\in[a,b]$;
3. $\mathsf M x''(t)=-\nabla_{x}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)$ for every $t\in[a,b]$.

Condition 3 is the model's equation of motion of the potential branch
([[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv)) written along the curve for the
presentation $(U,d)$ with the potential part alone: the residual forces $d$ do
not appear, and the statement is therefore a statement about the potential
part of the force map. No existence of curves satisfying these conditions is
asserted.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$ and $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]).
Assume the presentation has **no residual forces**, $d\equiv0$, so that the
force map itself is $F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)$. Then:

1. **motions are stationary.** If $x:J\to Q$ is a motion of the model on an
   interval $J$ with nonempty interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and
   $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subseteq J\cap I_{0}$, then the restriction $x|_{[a,b]}$
   is stationary for the action $S$ on $[a,b]$.

2. **stationary curves are restrictions of motions.** If $a<b$ with
   $[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$ and $x:[a,b]\to Q$ is a $C^{2}$ admissible curve that
   is stationary for $S$, then $x$ is the restriction to $[a,b]$ of the
   maximal motion of the model through the initial datum
   $\bigl(a,x(a),x'(a)\bigr)$ (whose existence and uniqueness are
   [[pthm-cm02-ivp]] clause 4); in particular the maximal interval of that
   motion contains $[a,b]$.

3. **identification.** Consequently the $C^{2}$ curves $x:[a,b]\to Q$ that are
   stationary for the action are exactly the restrictions to $[a,b]$ of the
   motions of the model whose maximal interval contains $[a,b]$, and the model
   equation satisfied is $\mathsf M x''=-\nabla_{x}U$ on that interval.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and on the declared
potential presentation with $d\equiv0$; it asserts no existence of stationary
curves for arbitrary endpoint data, no minimisation and no empirical value.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x_i'=Rx_i+\upsilon t+a_{0}\quad(i=1,\dots,N)$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},\upsilon\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); $\upsilon$ is the boost velocity
denoted by $v$ in that theorem. Define the block-diagonal map
$$R_{N}:=\operatorname{diag}(R,\dots,R):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$$
and the repeated tuples $\bar a_{0}:=(a_{0},\dots,a_{0})$ and
$\bar\upsilon:=(\upsilon,\dots,\upsilon)$ in $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$. Thus
$R_N x=(Rx_{1},\dots,Rx_{N})$, and the same componentwise rule applies to
velocities and forces; since $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3}$,
$R_N^{\mathsf T}R_N=I_{3N}$. If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of the
labels in the first frame, then the description of the same worldlines in the second
frame is
$$\eta(t'):=R_{N}x(t'-b)+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_{0}\qquad(t'\in J+b).$$
By clause 2 of the cited theorem, each $\eta_i$ is $C^{2}$ and
$\eta_i''(t')=R\ddot x_i(t'-b)$, so along the motion
$$m_i\eta_i''(t')=R F_i\bigl(t'-b,x(t'-b),\dot x(t'-b)\bigr).$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the force map below. Let $P$ be the inverse affine
transfer from new-frame data to old-frame data,
$$P(t',y,w):=\bigl(t'-b,\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}),\,R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\bigr).$$
Its preimage of the original domain is
$$D_{*}:=P^{-1}(D)=\{(t',y,w):P(t',y,w)\in D\};$$
it is open because $P$ is a homeomorphism and $D$ is open. Define
$$F_{*}:D_{*}\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad F_{*}(t',y,w):=R_N F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R_N^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-\bar\upsilon(t'-b)-\bar a_{0}\bigr),\ R_N^{\mathsf T}(w-\bar\upsilon)\Bigr).$$
The map $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its state variable:
the transfer and its inverse are affine, and at fixed time they act linearly
on state differences; on compact time intervals their state Lipschitz
constants are uniform, so precomposition preserves the stated regularity of
$F$. The framework
formulates the equation of motion in every inertial frame; a rule that does
not transform by this law is a description tied to the frame in which it was
written, and the framework attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When
$Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of the models of the companion page — the
transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a proper open $Q$ the
transferred position set $R_NQ+\bar\upsilon(t'-b)+\bar a_0$ may depend on
$t'$, and the equation is then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$ for the three independent *dimension symbols* of length, duration and mass. A **dimension** is an element of the free abelian group generated by $\ell,\tau,\mu$, that is, a triple $(a,b,c)\in\mathbb Z^3$ written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$; **products and inverses** of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, so that $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\cdot\ell^{a'}\tau^{b'}\mu^{c'}=\ell^{a+a'}\tau^{b+b'}\mu^{c+c'}$ and $(\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c})^{-1}=\ell^{-a}\tau^{-b}\mu^{-c}$. The **dimensionless** dimension is $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}$, abbreviated $1$.

**(b) The dimension map.** The conventions assign to the quantities of the framework a **dimension** $[X]$, subject to the rules

$$[XY]=[X][Y],\qquad [X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1},\qquad \left[\frac{dX}{du}\right]=[X][u]^{-1},$$

and to the requirement that a sum $X+Y$ is meaningful only when $[X]=[Y]$, in which case $[X+Y]=[X]$. The third rule applies to a differentiable dependence of a quantity $X$ on a quantity $u$ and covers iterated differentiation, so that $[d^{2}X/du^{2}]=[X][u]^{-2}$. The assignment is part of the conventions: the rules above are consistency requirements on it, not physical laws and not theorems.

**(c) Reference units.** The **metre** is the reference unit of length, the **second** the reference unit of duration and the **kilogram** the reference unit of mass. A quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\,\mathrm s^{b}\,\mathrm{kg}^{c}$: its value is a real multiple of that unit, and the conventions fix how the numerical value of a quantity is read (a coordinate value alone is a real number, and the unit declaration attaches its dimension). The coordinates of an adapted chart of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinate components $x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; the slice distance $d_{g}$ of [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] between simultaneous events is read in metres.

**(d) Typed quantity conventions.** The following constructions specify the quantities whose dimensions are recorded here, without adopting their dynamics. Fix a positive integer $N$, a nondegenerate open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with time parameter $t$ in seconds, position curves $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ with components in metres, and constant parameters $m_i>0$ in kilograms, for $1\le i\le N$. Derivatives and integrals have the meanings of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. These are conditional numerical constructions in a fixed spatial coordinate system; whether they represent a particular system is a separate model assumption.

1. **Velocity and acceleration** are the maps $w_i=x_i':I\to\mathbb R^3$ and $a_i=x_i'':I\to\mathbb R^3$, of dimensions $\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ componentwise.
2. The **mass operator** is the linear map $\mathsf M:(\mathbb R^3)^N\to(\mathbb R^3)^N$, $\mathsf M(z_1,\ldots,z_N)=(m_1z_1,\ldots,m_Nz_N)$, with dimension $\mu$; the **momentum** of label $i$ is $p_i=m_iw_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$, with component dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$.
3. A **force input** is a specified map $F:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, where $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open, its arguments are time, positions and velocities, and each output component has dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. No regularity or equation equating $F$ with $\mathsf M x''$ is adopted here. A later model must state both if needed.
4. For a specified scalar **potential energy** map $U:I\times O\to\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$ and a tuple $x(t)\in O$, the **kinetic energy** is $T(t)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N m_i\sum_{j=1}^3(w_i(t))_j^2$, and the **mechanical energy** is $E(t)=T(t)+U(t,x(t))$. Both are real-valued and have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}$; no conservation or applicability to every interaction is asserted.
5. Given a scalar map $L:I\times O\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ of the energy dimension and $t_0<t_1$ in $I$, assume $t\mapsto L(t,x(t),w(t))$ is integrable on $[t_0,t_1]$. Its **action on this curve segment** is the real number $S[x;t_0,t_1]=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}L(t,x(t),w(t))\,dt$, with dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (the integration convention multiplies the integrand's dimension by duration). No variational principle is imposed.
6. Relative to the chosen spatial origin, define the **angular momentum** $J_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ by $J_i(t)=x_i(t)\times p_i(t)$, where for $r,s\in\mathbb R^3$ the operation is explicitly $r\times s=(r_2s_3-r_3s_2,r_3s_1-r_1s_3,r_1s_2-r_2s_1)$. Its components have dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-1}$. These quantities depend on the chosen coordinates; dimensions alone assert no transformation or conservation law.
7. A **rotation matrix** here means a real $3\times3$ matrix $R$ satisfying $R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3$ and $\det R=1$; its entries are dimensionless. A radian angle is an arc length divided by its positive radius, hence dimensionless. A generalized coordinate means a component of a specified local coordinate chart on a configuration space; each such component has its own declared dimension, and only quantities of equal dimension are added.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any constant or parameter of a model is fixed by this item: in particular no mass, length or duration of any concrete system is asserted, and no measured value is recorded. Two numerical values that are equal but carry different dimensions are not thereby the same quantity. Where a treatment or a later item suppresses a dimensionful constant by a natural-unit convention, that convention is read as shorthand for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored, and it changes no dimension fixed here.

derivations.claim: Clause 1, motion as an Euler-Lagrange solution: let $x:J\to Q$ be a motion with $d\equiv0$. The interior $J^{\circ}$ is a nonempty open interval. For any $t_{0}\in J^{\circ}$ choose $a<b$ with $t_{0}\in(a,b)$ and $[a,b]\subseteq J^{\circ}$; the restriction $x|_{[a,b]}$ is a $C^{2}$ admissible curve of the chart instance and is stationary for the action of $L$ by [F4], so it satisfies $E_{L}(x)=0$ on $[a,b]$. As this holds for each $t_{0}\in J^{\circ}$, $E_{L}(x)=0$ throughout $J^{\circ}$.

Clause 2, differentiation: along any motion, $t\mapsto C(t,x(t),x'(t))$ is of class $C^{1}$ by [F6] and [F7], and differentiating $C=(\mathsf M x')\cdot\xi(t,x)-B(t,x)$ gives $$C'= igl(\mathsf M x'' igr)\cdot\xi+ igl(\mathsf M x' igr)\cdot D_{t}\xi-D_{t}B$$ at each $t\in J$. Substituting the strict identity of [F2] with $(t,x,v)=(t,x(t),x'(t))$, i.e. $D_{t}B=-
abla_{x}U\cdot\xi+(\mathsf M x')\cdot D_{t}\xi$, and then $\mathsf M x''=-
abla_{x}U+d$ from [F5], gives $$C'= igl(\mathsf M x'' igr)\cdot\xi+
abla_{x}U\cdot\xi= igl(\mathsf M x''+
abla_{x}U igr)\cdot\xi= igl\langle d(t,x(t),x'(t)),\xi(t,x(t)) igrangle.$$

Clause 1, conservation: by [F2] the pair $(\xi,B)$, with $\xi$ independent of $t$, is an infinitesimal point symmetry of the chart $(O,L)$. Step 1.1 shows that $x|_{J^{\circ}}$ is a $C^{2}$ curve on the open interval $J^{\circ}$ with graph in $O$ solving $E_{L}=0$, so the mathematical conservation theorem [F3] applies there and makes $t\mapsto L_{v}(t,x,x')\cdot\xi(x)-B(t,x)=(\mathsf M x'(t))\cdot\xi(x(t))-B(t,x(t))$ constant on $J^{\circ}$. The charge is continuous on $J$ by [F7]; every endpoint of $J$ that belongs to $J$ is a limit of points of $J^{\circ}$, so continuity gives the same constant value there. Thus the charge is constant on $J$.

Clause 2, conservation criterion: by step 1.2 the derivative of $t\mapsto C(t,x(t),x'(t))$ is the pairing displayed there; by [F6] a $C^{1}$ function on the interval $J$ is constant on $J$ if and only if its derivative vanishes everywhere on $J$, so $C$ is constant on $J$ exactly when the pairing vanishes for every $t\in J$.

Clause 1 is steps 1.1 and 2.1, and clause 2 is steps 1.2 and 2.2; both clauses are conditional deductions from the indicated hypotheses, and no claim of existence of a symmetry datum or of empirical content is made.

boundaries.reason: The statement quantifies over no possibly empty family: the model data are finite (N>=1 labels), the state domain is a product, and no union or limit over an empty index set occurs.

boundaries.evidence: Zero data are included: d identically 0 is clause 1, and along a motion with d=0 the pairing in clause 2 vanishes; no positivity of the charge or of the generator is used. See steps 1.2 and 2.2.
The N=1 case is included: all displays are sums over 1<=i<=N and the argument never uses N>=2. See step 1.2.
Degenerate data are excluded by the hypotheses: masses m_i>0 by the model data, J has nonempty interior by hypothesis, and the charge is defined on the open chart domain. See Statement.

The assertions are on the interval J: step 1.1 restricts a motion to closed subintervals contained in J with the interior Euler-Lagrange theorem and extends to all of J, and step 2.2 applies the interior constancy criterion on J. See steps 1.1 and 2.2.

boundaries.reason: The symmetry triple (0,xi,B) and the motion are given. Step 1.1 takes a compact subinterval around one fixed interior time to apply the charge supplier; step 1.2 computes the charge directly and step 2.1 extends constancy to included endpoints by continuity. These pointwise applications do not assemble a simultaneous selection of neighbourhoods or construct symmetry data.

boundaries.evidence: Clause 2's forward reading (the pairing vanishes everywhere on J, hence C is constant) is step 2.2, using the derivative formula of step 1.2.
Clause 2's reverse reading (C is constant on J, hence the pairing vanishes everywhere) is step 2.2, using that a C^1 function constant on the interval J has vanishing derivative at every point of J.

risk_review.notes: Checked five steps: strict identity substitutes to C prime=d·xi, including time-dependent xi in the rate clause; the conservation supplier requires time-independent xi, C1 data and a chart interval inside the nonempty motion interior, all available. Endpoint values follow by continuity; constancy iff pairing vanishes follows from the interval theorem and one-sided derivatives. No converse from conservation or empirical assertion. Model data are C2 so the definition reverse-regularity correction does not affect this use. Local source review: Tong official Section 2.4–2.4.1 supplies the strict coordinate case; SICM official ZIP §1.8.5 and §§5.4.4–5.4.5 supplies coordinate symmetry, rotating Hamiltonian and gauge context; Likharev current §2.3–2.4 checked.
